title: 5 Rules for a JEE/NEET Study Timetable That Doesn't Burn You Out
description: Almost every JEE and NEET timetable dies within a few weeks. Five rules for a structure that survives real life, with separate weekly rotations for JEE and NEET and a daily block template.
author: Studyloaf Team

content.body: Most JEE and NEET timetables die the same way. Five subjects a day, a mock every Sunday, no gaps. It looks impressive on paper and falls apart within two weeks, usually after one bad day turns into three. That isn't a willpower problem. It's a design problem: the plan assumed every day would go perfectly. Here are five rules for a structure that holds up, with separate weekly rotations for JEE and NEET, because the two exams weight their subjects very differently.

content.heading: Rule 1: Match subjects to your energy, not to the clock
list: Spend three days noticing when you focus best, without changing anything. Most students find one or two clear high-energy windows, often morning or late afternoon
Put your hardest work in those windows: new chapters or problem sets in your weakest subject
Use low-energy time for work that doesn't need fresh thinking: revising formula sheets, NCERT rereads, flashcards, or reviewing yesterday's mistakes
Don't fight your body clock to copy a topper's 5 am routine. A timetable you can keep beats an impressive one you can't

content.heading: Rule 2: Fix the weekly rotation in advance
content.body: Deciding every morning what to study drains energy before you've started, and it quietly favours whichever subject feels easiest. Set the rotation once, so the only daily decision is to begin. The rotation has to fit your exam. JEE gives Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics 100 marks each, so they get roughly equal time, tilted towards your weakest. NEET gives Biology 360 of 720 marks, as much as Physics and Chemistry together, so Biology appears almost every day.

content.body: Swap the subjects to match your own weak spots, but keep the shape: new material in your best hours, practice next, and one day a week for a mock and a proper review of it.

content.heading: Rule 3: Leave real slack
list: A timetable with zero buffer has zero room for a bad day, and bad days are guaranteed
Leave one unscheduled block every day, about an hour. On a good day it becomes extra practice; on a bad day it absorbs the overrun
Keep one lighter day a week, so a missed block has somewhere to go
Slack is what stops a bad day becoming a bad week

content.heading: Rule 4: Give revision its own fixed slot
list: Revision isn't what happens if there's time left over. New chapters you can't recall on exam day are wasted hours
Fix it as a daily slot, such as the last 45 minutes of the day, plus one longer session at the end of each week
Use spaced review: look at a chapter again a day after you study it, then about a week later, then a month later
Treat the slot as non-negotiable, the same as a class

content.heading: Rule 5: Take one full day off every week
list: Not a lighter day. Off
Students who skip rest for weeks don't save time; they lose several days to a crash later
A day off is also when the week's material settles. Coming back after a break is part of how it sticks
It's the rule people cut first and regret most

content.heading: A daily template that uses all five rules
content.body: For a full study day of about 7 to 8 hours (fewer on school or college days, with the same order):

table.caption: One study day, in blocks
rows: Today's hardest work from the weekly rotation
Practice set or the second subject
Formula sheets, NCERT rereads, error log
Whatever overran today, or extra practice

content.heading: Common mistakes
list: Copying someone else's timetable instead of building around your own energy and weak subjects
Giving NEET Biology the same time as Physics and Chemistry, when it carries half the marks
Planning every hour of every day, so the first bad day breaks the whole week
Taking a weekly mock but skipping the review, which is where most of its value is

content.body: None of this is complicated. It's permission to build a plan you can keep.
